title: Fire safety
blurb: The fire triangle, extinguisher colours and uses, and how to evacuate a practice when patients are reclined in the chair.
question: The fire alarm sounds while the dentist is preparing a cavity and the patient is fully reclined. A colleague says a small fire has started in a bin next to an electrical socket in the corridor. What do you do first, and which extinguishers would be safe on that fire if a trained person tackles it?

teach.h: Fire safety is a legal duty
teach.body: In England and Wales, the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005 makes a 'responsible person', usually the employer or owner, carry out a fire risk assessment and put precautions in place: alarms and detection, clear escape routes, signs, extinguishers, staff training and drills. Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own equivalent fire safety laws. Every member of the team must know the practice fire procedure, because in a fire there is no time to learn it.

In the UK, extinguisher bodies are red; a coloured band or panel shows the type.

teach.caption: Don't hold a CO₂ horn: it gets cold enough to burn the skin. In a small room, CO₂ displaces the air you breathe and powder cuts visibility. Fire classes: A solids, B liquids, C gases, F cooking oils.

teach.h: Only fight a fire if it is safe
teach.body: Your first job is always to raise the alarm. Only tackle a fire if you are trained, it is small, you have the right extinguisher, and you have a clear escape route behind you. If it doesn't go out quickly, leave and close the door behind you. A fire blanket can smother a very small fire, such as burning clothing. Never put yourself at risk to save equipment.

teach.body: Dental patients may be reclined, numb, anxious, sedated or have limited mobility. Remove instruments and any rubber dam, bring the chair upright, and guide the patient out calmly. Patients who need help to evacuate, such as wheelchair users, should have a plan agreed in advance (a personal emergency evacuation plan). The appointment list helps the fire marshal check everyone is out.

teach.text: Fire exits and escape routes must be kept clear AT ALL TIMES, not just when an inspection is due. Deliveries stacked by a rear door, or a fire door wedged open, can cost lives.

items: Fire triangle: heat, fuel, oxygen. Remove one to put the fire out.
Extinguisher labels: water red, foam cream, CO₂ black, powder blue, wet chemical yellow.
Electrical fire: CO₂ (or dry powder). Never water or foam.
Raise the alarm first. Only fight a small fire if trained and with an escape route.
Evacuate: sit patients up, help them out, close doors, no lifts, assembly point, don't re-enter.

summary: You can now explain the fire triangle, name the five extinguisher types by colour and use, choose a safe extinguisher for an electrical fire, and evacuate patients safely, including those reclined in the dental chair.

A.q: A small fire starts in a curing light's power supply. Which extinguisher is most suitable?
A.why: CO₂ is suitable for electrical fires: it smothers the fire, doesn't conduct electricity and leaves no residue.

whyNot.0: Water conducts electricity and must never be used on electrical fires.
whyNot.1: Foam is water-based and not suitable for live electrical equipment.
whyNot.3: Wet chemical is designed for cooking oil and fat fires.

A.q: Deliveries have been stacked in front of the rear fire exit. Why must this be cleared at once?
options: To allow safe escape in an emergency
To keep the delivery route tidy
To meet the terms of the lease
To let air circulate in the building
A.why: Fire exits and escape routes must be kept clear at all times so everyone can get out quickly.

whyNot.1: Tidiness is a side benefit; the legal reason is safe escape.
whyNot.2: The lease isn't the reason; fire safety law requires clear exits.
whyNot.3: Ventilation is not the purpose of a fire exit.

A.q: What are the three elements of the fire triangle?
A.why: A fire needs heat, fuel and oxygen. Remove any one and it goes out.

whyNot.1: Smoke is a product of fire, not one of its ingredients.
whyNot.2: A spark is one source of heat, and smoke is a product, not an element.
whyNot.3: Water is used to put fires out; it isn't part of the triangle.

B.q: A dry powder extinguisher can be identified by which colour band?
B.why: Dry powder extinguishers have a blue label or band on a red body.

B.q: The fire alarm sounds during treatment and the patient is fully reclined. What should you do?
options: Sit the patient up and guide them out
Leave the patient and evacuate alone
Wait in the surgery for the fire marshal's instructions
B.why: Stop treatment, remove instruments, bring the patient upright and guide them out safely.

whyNot.0: Treatment must stop; there is no time to finish.
whyNot.2: Patients rely on the team to get them out safely.
whyNot.3: Waiting wastes vital time; follow the evacuation procedure.

B.q: Why should oxygen cylinders be kept away from oil and grease?
options: Grease makes cylinders hard to grip
B.why: Oxygen doesn't burn itself, but it makes oil, grease and other materials ignite easily and burn intensely.

whyNot.0: The danger is fire, not a blocked valve.
whyNot.1: Grip matters for handling, but the main danger is fire.
whyNot.3: Stained labels are not the safety concern.

C.q: Which extinguisher should NEVER be used on a fire involving electrical equipment?
C.why: Water conducts electricity, so using it on electrical fires risks electrocution.

whyNot.0: CO₂ is the usual choice for electrical fires.
whyNot.1: Dry powder can be used on electrical fires, though it is messy and not ideal in small rooms.
whyNot.3: Water is unsafe on electrical fires.

C.q: During an evacuation, which action is correct?
options: Use the lift to move patients faster
Collect your bag from the staff room
Close doors behind you as you leave
Go back in to check the surgery
C.why: Closing doors slows the spread of fire and smoke. Then go straight to the assembly point.

whyNot.0: Lifts must not be used in a fire unless they are designated evacuation lifts.
whyNot.3: Never re-enter until the fire service says it is safe.

C.q: A colleague says they will tackle a fire. When is it reasonable to do so?
options: When it is large but contained to one room
When trained, it's small and escape is clear
Whenever an extinguisher is close by
Before the alarm has been raised
C.why: Only tackle a fire if you're trained, it's small, you have the right extinguisher and a clear escape route, after raising the alarm.

whyNot.0: A large fire is beyond what an extinguisher can safely deal with.
whyNot.2: Being close to an extinguisher doesn't make it safe to use.
whyNot.3: The alarm must always be raised first.

reteach.title: Think of fire as a three-legged stool
reteach.question: A three-legged stool falls over if you kick away any one leg. How does that help you choose an extinguisher and spot fire risks?

blocks.body: The legs are heat, fuel and oxygen. Water kicks away heat by cooling. Foam and CO₂ kick away oxygen by smothering. Good housekeeping kicks away fuel before a fire starts: clear waste, store flammables properly. In a dental practice, extra oxygen from cylinders makes the stool sturdier, which is why cylinders are kept away from heat and grease.

blocks.text: Black = CO₂ = electrics. Red = water = never on electrics.

explain.body: Fire needs heat, fuel and oxygen. Prevention means controlling all three: safe electrics (heat), tidy waste and stored flammables (fuel), and careful oxygen cylinder storage.

test.q: Emptying full waste bins at the end of each session mainly reduces which side of the fire triangle?
test.why: Paper and waste are fuel. Removing them takes away something to burn.

whyNot.0: Heat sources are things like faulty sockets and heaters.
whyNot.1: Oxygen comes from the air and cylinders.
whyNot.3: Smoke is a product of fire, not part of the triangle.

explain.body: All UK extinguishers have red bodies with a coloured band: water red, foam cream, CO₂ black, dry powder blue, wet chemical yellow.

test.q: An extinguisher has a cream band. What type is it?

explain.body: Water and foam: paper, wood and fabric (foam also covers flammable liquids), but never electrics. CO₂: electrical fires. Dry powder: most fires including electrical, but avoid in small enclosed rooms. Wet chemical: cooking oil and fat.

test.q: Which extinguisher is designed for cooking oil and fat fires in a staff kitchen?
test.why: Wet chemical extinguishers are designed for class F (cooking oil and fat) fires.

whyNot.0: CO₂ is mainly for electrical fires and can spread burning oil.
whyNot.2: Water on burning oil causes a violent flare-up.
whyNot.3: Foam is not the right choice for deep cooking oil fires.

explain.body: Raise the alarm, stop treatment and sit the patient up, guide everyone out, close doors, don't use lifts or stop for belongings, go to the assembly point for a roll call, and never re-enter until told it's safe.

test.q: Why does a dental nurse need to know the evacuation procedure in detail?
options: Fire drills count as verifiable CPD
It is checked at every appraisal
The fire service inspects the practice every year
Patients may need help out of the chair
test.why: Patients may be reclined, numb or anxious and rely on the team to get them out safely.

whyNot.0: Fire drills are not the reason; patient safety is.
whyNot.2: Inspection is not the reason; being able to act in a real fire is.
